CA1 · PYRAMIDAL & PRINCIPAL CELLS

CA1 pyramidal cell mpg141209_A

Where: Soma in stratum pyramidale; basal dendrites in oriens, apical dendrite through radiatum to lacunosum-moleculare

Role in the circuit: Main output of the hippocampus. Integrates CA3 input (Schaffer collaterals, middle dendrites) with entorhinal input (distal tuft) and projects to subiculum and entorhinal cortex.

Species: Rat

How it was recorded and reconstructed: Filled during whole-cell recording in hippocampal slices, imaged and traced in Neurolucida, with the layer boundaries traced too.

Model: Migliore et al. (2018) PLoS Comput Biol 14:e1006423. Data-driven multicompartment models; ion-channel densities optimised to each cell’s recordings. Open ModelDB 244688 ↗

	REGION	LAYER	LENGTH	MAIN INPUT / ROLE
	Axon	oriens → alveus, to subiculum and entorhinal cortex	1490 µm	Output. Axo-axonic cells inhibit its initial segment.
	Basal dendrites	stratum oriens	4076 µm (46% of dendrite)	CA3 Schaffer collaterals and CA1 recurrent collaterals
	Apical trunk & oblique dendrites	stratum radiatum	2574 µm (29% of dendrite)	CA3 Schaffer collaterals

WHAT YOU ARE SEEING

Press Fire a spike at the soma. The action potential runs out along the axon (it regenerates, so it stays full size) and back into the dendrites (a backpropagating spike, which fades with distance). Or click a dendrite and send in a synaptic input: it spreads passively and shrinks on the way to the soma.

03 · QUANTIFY

Morphometrics lab: compare any two cells

Every cell is measured with the same code (dendrites only, so trimmed long-range axons do not distort the numbers). The Sholl analysis counts how many dendritic branches cross spheres of growing radius around the soma, the standard way to compare dendritic complexity. Try the entorhinal wild-type vs 3xTg-AD pair, or a CA1 pyramidal cell vs a Purkinje cell.

Pyramidal cells have one long apical dendrite crossing several layers, so inputs from different pathways land at different distances from the soma.
Granule cells have a cone of dendrites in one layer (the molecular layer) and no basal dendrites in adult rodents.
Interneurons often have more axon than dendrite, spread densely in the layer they target: perisomatic (basket), axon initial segment (axo-axonic) or distal dendrites (O-LM).

02 · IDEAS TO TRY

Questions this lab can answer
Is the bAP limited by channels or by shape? Run Back-propagating spike on two CA1 cells, then set A-type to 0×. Use Keep as reference to overlay runs.
Where are dendritic spikes born? Clustered tuft input with Na⁺ on, then put Local TTX on the apical trunk only.
Does a branch matter? Cut branch on an oblique or the tuft and rerun the firing protocol: input resistance and rate change.
Ih and AD. Aβ reduces dendritic A-type current (Chen 2005) and HCN changes are reported in AD models. Compare Aβ-like, ZD7288 and published presets on the sag and bAP protocols.
Shunting inhibition. Put a GABA-A synapse at the soma and AMPA synapses in the tuft; move the GABA synapse onto the trunk and compare.
Other cell types. The channel set is the CA1 pyramidal one, so granule cells, interneurons and cortical cells are what-if experiments: same channels, different shape.

Under the hood equations, numerics and the check against NEURON
Cable equation per compartment

\(C_i\,\dfrac{dV_i}{dt} = -\sum_{\text{ion}} g_{\text{ion},i}(V_i - E_{\text{ion}}) - g_L(V_i-E_L) + \sum_{j\in\text{nb}(i)} g_{ij}(V_j - V_i) + I_{\text{inj}} + I_{\text{syn}}\)

\(g_{ij}^{-1} = \dfrac{R_a L_i}{2\pi r_i^2} + \dfrac{R_a L_j}{2\pi r_j^2}\) (half-compartments in series). Areas use the frustum surface of each traced segment.

Backward Euler for \(V\) (unconditionally stable) solved in \(O(N)\) with Hines elimination on the tree; gates advance by exponential Euler: \(x \leftarrow x_\infty + (x - x_\infty)e^{-\Delta t/\tau_x}\), Δt = 0.025 ms.

Synapses: \(g(t) = \bar g\,\eta\,(e^{-t/\tau_2}-e^{-t/\tau_1})\); AMPA 0.2/2 ms, NMDA 2/50 ms with \(B(V)=1/(1+e^{-0.062V}[\text{Mg}^{2+}]/3.57)\), GABA-A 0.5/8 ms (E = −75 mV), GABA-B 30/150 ms (E = −90 mV). AMPA + NMDA uses an NMDA:AMPA conductance ratio of 0.8.

02 · IDEAS

Experiments to try
Where does inhibition work best? In Feed-forward inhibition, change the PV → CA1 target from perisomatic to distal dendrites; compare CA1 spike count and latency.
AIS veto window. In Chandelier → AIS, shift the chandelier drive earlier or later than the pyramidal spikes; compare with the NEURON maps on the axo-axonic page.
NMDA and dendritic location. In CA3 → CA1, switch AMPA + NMDA to AMPA only, then move the contacts from mid to distal dendrites.
Morphology as a variable. Keep the wiring, swap the target for another CA1 reconstruction (cells are interchangeable in the list).
Jump before flight. In Fly escape, compare when the TTMn and the wing motor neuron fire, then remove PSI → wing motor neuron: the jump survives, the flight output goes (as in flies lacking the PSI pathway).
Why motoneurons need many inputs. In Corticospinal cell → spinal motoneuron, delete the motoneuron's steady input, then raise the number of contacts until one cortical cell can fire it alone; compare with the other motoneurons in the list (Cells tab).
AD-related changes. Set a pyramidal cell's profile to Aβ-like or swap the wild-type entorhinal cell for the 3xTg-AD one in EC → DG.

Look: colour by compartment or path distance; turn labels (legend, scale bar, region) on or off; choose whether the title is the neuron’s name, your own text, or nothing.

MY RESEARCH · MODEL · CEBALLOS, CHADLY, LOWET & PENA 2025
Model ladder: one cell at six levels of realism

CA1-like neurons can resonate twice: single spikes lock best to one input frequency and bursts to another, and the two preferences interleave across theta and gamma. This page rebuilds the paper’s model step by step: a two-point leaky integrate-and-fire cell, the Allen Institute’s generalized LIF (GLIF), a two-dimensional adaptive exponential model (AdEx), and finally the full biophysical two-compartment model with the paper’s conductances. Every rung gets the same θ + γ input and the same single-spike/burst analysis.

02 · MEASURE

Single-spike and burst resonance

The paper’s central measurement: drive the cell with one sinusoid at a time (on top of Iapp) and count, for each frequency, how many single-spike events and how many burst events occur per second (first spike of each event). The peak of each curve is that firing mode’s resonant frequency; the paper compares them with Δf = fSS − fBS and ΔA = ASS − ABS.

03 · THE LADDER

What each rung adds
RUNG	STATE VARIABLES	WHAT IT CAN DO	WHAT IT CANNOT
Two-point LIF	Vsoma, Vdend	Low-pass filtering, dendritic attenuation (gac), firing-rate locking	No subthreshold resonance, no bursts: nothing slower than τm = C/gL = 25 ms
GLIF 1–5 (Teeter et al. 2018)	V, three after-spike currents, two threshold variables	Adaptation, rebound, bursting from a depolarising after-spike current, spike-shaped thresholds; fits recordings with few parameters	Currents are triggered by spikes only: no voltage-dependent subthreshold resonance
2-D NaP + Iₕ (Pena & Rotstein 2022)	V, r	Biophysical subthreshold resonance from the two currents the lab studies; amplification by NaP	Spikes only via an added threshold/reset; no bursts
2-D AdEx (Brette & Gerstner 2005)	V, w	Exponential spike onset: for INa ∝ m∞³ the spike-initiation slope is ΔT ≈ σm/3 = 9.5/3 ≈ 3.2 mV (Fourcaud-Trocmé et al. 2003); the f–I fit used here gives 4.4 mV because w and the other currents also bend the onset, subthreshold resonance when a > 0 and τw is slow (an IM/Iₕ stand-in), bursting with a high reset	One slow process stands in for KM, sKCa and Iₕ together
Minimal bursting (Lowet et al. 2023)	7: Vs, m, n, h, Vd, NaP gate, KS gate	Dendritic bursts from NaP + slow K⁺; theta-locked bursts and gamma-locked single spikes as in the voltage imaging	No Ca²⁺ currents, no Iₕ
Biophysical HH (Ceballos et al. 2025)	11: Vs, h, n, b, z, r, c, [Ca²⁺], q, Vd, hₕ	Every current of the paper, Ca²⁺-dependent K⁺, dendritic Iₕ	Single dendrite, no morphology, parameters partly ambiguous (below)

Fitting the reduced models to the biophysical one (as the Allen Institute fit GLIFs to recordings). Subthreshold parameters come from the linearisation (Reduce); spiking parameters are fitted by differential evolution to the HH model’s f–I curve (0–6 µA/cm²) and its single-spike and burst rates under a 2 µA/cm² sinusoid at 4, 8, 12, 16, 25, 40 and 70 Hz. Press Load fit to the HH model on the AdEx or GLIF rung.

HH (target)	15 · 27 · 52	8 · 12 · 16	25 · 30 · 18	—
AdEx fit	21 · 29 · 49	0 · 12 · 16	25 · 40 · 23	ΔT 4.4 mV, VT −51.8, b 0.88, Vr −68.7 (a 0.578, τw 75 ms from GDerM)

The AdEx, whose w is literally the linearised IM, captures the f–I curve and the burst band at 12–16 Hz but misses 8 Hz bursts. The GLIF, with no subthreshold resonance, reproduces the f–I curve less well near threshold and bursts only at the slowest frequencies: its after-spike currents are triggered by spikes, not by the input’s phase. A rung that keeps both a voltage-driven slow variable and spike-triggered currents is the natural next model.

Theta resonance in real CA1 dendrites

CA1 pyramidal dendrites prefer theta-range inputs, and the preferred frequency rises with distance from the soma because h channels get denser. This page takes a published, data-tuned h-channel model, checks it against the authors’ own output, then runs it on five other real CA1 cells to see how much of the resonance map comes from the h-channel gradient and how much from morphology.

04 · MODEL DETAILS

Under the hood
Under the hood channel, gradients, how the trunk is found, protocol
MEMBRANE

\(C_m\dot V=-g_{pas}(V-E_{pas})-\bar g_h\,l\,(V-E_h)+I_{chirp}\), with \(\tau_l(V)\dot l=l_\infty(V)-l\) (Magee-type h kinetics from the authors’ h.mod, q10 = 4.5, 34 °C, Eh = −30 mV). Epas is set per segment so that −65 mV is the steady state.

GRADIENTS (D = STRAIGHT-LINE DISTANCE FROM THE SOMA)
\(\bar g_h(d)=34\,\mu S/cm^2\,\left(1+\frac{100}{1+e^{-(d-380)/34}}\right)\) on the trunk
V½: −82 mV up to 100 µm, then falling linearly to −90 mV at 300 µm
Rm = 200 kΩ·cm² falling sigmoidally to 12 kΩ·cm² (midpoint 200 µm); Ra 50 → 35 Ω·cm
Obliques inherit the trunk values at their branch point; soma and basal dendrites use the base values.
FINDING THE TRUNK IN A NEW CELL

Start at the apical root section with the most dendrite below it, then repeatedly step into the child branch with the largest total subtree length until reaching a tip. This follows the main shaft into the tuft, as the hand-picked trunk does in the original model.

PROTOCOL

Linear chirp 0.5 → 20 Hz over 9.6 s, 20 pA, injected and recorded at the same location (local impedance). \(|Z(f)|=|\mathcal F\{V\}/\mathcal F\{I\}|\), averaged in 0.25 Hz bins. fR is the frequency at peak |Z|, Q = |Z(fR)| / |Z(0.5 Hz)|. Fixed step 0.1 ms.

LIMITS

The gradients were tuned to the authors’ cell, so on other cells they are a hypothesis. There is no M-current (which supports somatic resonance near −60 mV; Hu et al. 2002) and no spines. Diameters of the SEU–Allen cell are not measured (constant), so its curve reflects branching only.

05 · FOR YOUR CA1 RESONANCE PROJECT

What this lets you test
Main finding: the published gradient does not transfer as-is. With identical gradients, somatic fR ranges from about 4 Hz (n5038804) to about 9 Hz (the long Jarsky cell), against about 3 Hz in recordings. The gradient is defined in absolute µm, so longer cells place much more of their membrane in the high-h region, and that extra h current loads the soma.
Normalising distance doesn't fix it: rescaling each trunk to the original cell's length brings the soma down to about 3–5 Hz, but then the distal rise disappears (about 4 Hz at 300 µm instead of about 9 Hz). Neither rule reproduces the data across cells. The h-channel distribution has to be fitted per cell, or defined by something other than distance (for example dendritic diameter or branch order). This is a concrete, testable question for your project.
Morphology vs channels: any AD-vs-control comparison of resonance needs matched morphology or per-cell fits. Otherwise cell size alone can shift fR by several Hz.
AD-like h-channel loss (0.5×) or LTP-like gain (1.5×): Narayanan & Johnston showed that LTP increases h current and raises fR across the dendritic tree. Toggle the density to see the predicted shift in every cell.
Link to your two-compartment model: fit your soma/dendrite compartments to the 0 µm and 300 µm curves of one cell here. This turns the reduced model into one with measured spatial anchors.
Next experiment in silico: add the M-current at the soma and repeat at −60 mV, where the two resonance mechanisms (h and M) separate (Hu et al. 2002).

04 · MODEL DETAILS

Under the hood
Under the hood channels, gradients, stimulus and numerics
MEMBRANE

\(C_m\frac{dV}{dt} = -g_{pas}(V-E_{pas}) - \bar g_{Na}m^3h\,(V-E_{Na}) - \bar g_{Kdr}n^4(V-E_K) - \bar g_{KA}\,a\,b\,(V-E_K) - \bar g_h\,l\,(V-E_h) + I\)

Rm = 28 kΩ·cm², Cm = 1 µF/cm², Ra = 150 Ω·cm (axon 50). ENa = 55, EK = −90, Eh = −30 mV. Temperature 35 °C. Epas is set per segment so that every compartment starts at steady state at −65 mV, as in the original code.

DISTRIBUTIONS (D = PATH DISTANCE FROM SOMA)
Na⁺ (na3): 25 mS/cm², uniform in soma and dendrites; axon nax 5× higher.
Kdr: 10 mS/cm², uniform.
A-type K⁺: proximal form (kap) for d ≤ 100 µm and distal form (kad) beyond, both \(30\,(1+d/100)\) mS/cm² × the scale you choose.
Ih: \(0.05\,(1+3d/100)\) mS/cm², with half-activation −73 mV proximally and −81 mV distally.
STIMULUS & NUMERICS

Somatic current step of 2.5 nA for 1.5 ms (one spike). Variable-step CVODE, 20 ms run, d_λ = 0.1 at 50 Hz for segmentation. Peak V per segment is recorded with the authors’ ds mechanism. Cells without a usable traced axon get a standard 200 µm, 1 µm-diameter axon carrying the axonal channels. Long-range MouseLight and SEU–Allen axons are replaced by that stub so they do not dominate run time.

LIMITS

This is one published parameter set, tuned to one cell, applied to others. Real cells vary in channel density, spine density (spines add membrane and are not modelled here) and dendritic Na⁺ inactivation during trains. The point is the relative effect of morphology, not exact millivolts.

Not a subthreshold model. I also ran 0.5–20 Hz ZAP (chirp) currents to look for Ih resonance. At rest this channel set has a somatic input impedance of only about 10–15 MΩ (n5038804), well below typical CA1 recordings, because the large A-type and Kdr conductances are partly open at −65 mV. Its impedance profile shows no theta resonance. So use this model for bAPs and a resonance-tuned model (for example your two-compartment CA1 model, or Ih/M-current models fitted to impedance data) for theta questions.

05 · RESEARCH QUESTIONS

What could you test with this?
Strong vs weak propagation. Golding, Kath & Spruston (2001) found that distal bAP amplitude in CA1 is bimodal across cells. Does any of these morphologies switch between regimes with a modest A-type change, while others do not?
Obliques vs trunk. Migliore et al. (2005) showed that local oblique geometry shapes propagation. Colour the map and compare obliques with trunk segments at the same distance.
Alzheimer’s link. A-type K⁺ (Kv4.2) loss and dendritic hyperexcitability are reported in AD models (for example tau-dependent Kv4.2 depletion; Hall et al. 2015). Scaling A-type to 0.5× gives a first-pass prediction of how much further bAPs would invade, and so how plasticity (which needs bAP–EPSP coincidence) might change.
Your resonance project. The Ih gradient is the same one that sets dendritic theta resonance. A next step is to run chirp-current impedance profiles on these five cells.

KEY TERMS

Four ideas this page uses
KEY TERM	MEANING HERE
INaP (persistent Na⁺)	A small Na⁺ current that activates instantly near −50 mV and does not inactivate. It adds a steady inward push below spike threshold.
IM (M-type K⁺, Kv7/KCNQ)	A slowly activating, non-inactivating K⁺ current (τ = 75 ms here). It builds up during firing and decays during silence: the model’s only slow variable, z.
Fast–slow analysis	Freeze the slow variable, find what the fast system does at each value (rest or spike), then let the slow variable move.
Square-wave burst	A burst that starts when rest disappears (a fold, or saddle-node) and ends when the spiking orbit collides with a saddle (homoclinic); rest and spiking coexist in between (bistability).

02 · WHY IT BURSTS

The fast–slow phase plane

The M-current gate z is about 100× slower than every other variable. So treat z as a fixed parameter and ask what the other four variables (V, h, n, b) do for each value. The answer is the black curve below: for each z, the voltages where the cell can rest (solid where stable, dashed where unstable). Where rest is unstable or absent, the cell spikes: the purple band shows the highest and lowest voltage of that repetitive firing. Now release z. The red trajectory is the full model.

Figure 2. Fast–slow analysis of the zero-Ca²⁺ model with the current parameters. Black: steady states of the fast subsystem with z frozen (solid stable, dashed unstable). Purple: maximum and minimum V of repetitive spiking with z frozen. Green: the z-nullcline z = z∞(V); above it z decays, below it z grows. Red: the full trajectory (last 1.5 s). How a burst works: during silence the cell sits on the lower stable branch and z decays (moves left) until that branch ends at a fold (knee); the cell jumps to spiking. Spiking keeps V mostly above the green curve so z grows (moves right) until the spiking branch ends, and the cell falls back to rest. Rest and spiking coexist over the middle range of z: that bistability is what makes the burst.

Why weakening IM stops bursting in the model. IM is the only slow variable: it builds up during firing and ends the burst. Weaken it and the spiking branch reaches further right than z can ever climb, so firing never stops (tonic); remove it and the cell can end up stuck depolarised. Experiments are more nuanced: in CA1 slices, partial M-channel block enhances the spike afterdepolarisation and can promote bursting (Yue & Yaari 2004). A one-compartment model with one fixed parameter set captures one burst mechanism, not every condition. Why INaP is neither necessary nor sufficient (the paper’s conclusion): more INaP induces bursting and adds spikes per burst, but the pattern map below also shows bursts with gNaP = 0 at low gM, and tonic firing or silence at large gNaP. The paper adds that IM-driven bursting needs spike-generating kinetics that are fast, but not extremely fast: try φ in Under the hood.

04 · KEY EQUATIONS

The model in five lines

Current balance for one compartment (units: mV, ms, mS/cm², µA/cm²):

\[ C_m\frac{dV}{dt} = -g_L(V-V_L) - I_{NaT} - I_{NaP} - I_{Kdr} - I_A - I_M\;[-\,I_{Ca} - I_C - I_{AHP}] + I_{app} \]

\[ I_{NaT}=g_{Na}\,m_\infty^3(V)\,h\,(V-V_{Na}),\quad I_{NaP}=g_{NaP}\,p_\infty(V)\,(V-V_{Na}) \]

\[ I_{Kdr}=g_{Kdr}\,n^4(V-V_K),\quad I_A=g_A\,a_\infty^3(V)\,b\,(V-V_K),\quad I_M=g_M\,z\,(V-V_K) \]

\[ \frac{dz}{dt}=\frac{z_\infty(V)-z}{\tau_z},\qquad x_\infty(V)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-(V-\theta_x)/\sigma_x}} \]

Sodium activation and A-type activation are instantaneous; h and n relax with voltage-dependent time constants scaled by φ = 10. In normal Ca²⁺ the model adds a high-threshold Ca²⁺ current, a fast Ca²⁺- and voltage-activated K⁺ current (IC, BK-like) and a slow Ca²⁺-activated AHP current (τq = 450 ms), with Ca²⁺ decaying with τCa = 13 ms.

GATE	Θ (MV)	Σ (MV)	TIME CONSTANT
m (NaT activation)	−30	9.5	instantaneous
h (NaT inactivation)	−45	−7	(1 + 7.5 Γ(V, −40.5, −6)) / φ
p (NaP)	−47 (zero Ca) / −41 (normal)	3	instantaneous
n (Kdr)	−35	10	(1 + 5 Γ(V, −27, −15)) / φ
a, b (A-type)	−50, −80	20, −6	instantaneous, 15 ms
z (M)	−39	5	75 ms

Worked example: the resting point. With the zero-Ca²⁺ set and no applied current, every gate sits at its steady state and the currents balance near −71.8 mV (the authors’ initial condition). There, p∞ = 1/(1 + e(71.8−47)/3) ≈ 2.6 × 10⁻⁴, so INaP ≈ 0.3 × 2.6 × 10⁻⁴ × (−126.8) ≈ −0.01 µA/cm²: negligible at rest. At −55 mV p∞ ≈ 0.065, giving about −2 µA/cm², larger than the 0.66 µA/cm² applied current. That steep rise between rest and threshold is what lets INaP amplify depolarisation.

06 · WHAT THE MODEL LEAVES OUT

Limits of a one-compartment model
No dendrites. Real CA1 bursts often involve dendritic Ca²⁺ spikes and back-propagation. The paper motivates a somatic model experimentally: in low Ca²⁺, bursting persisted after the apical dendrites were cut off. Bursting in intact cells with normal Ca²⁺ needs the dendrites too.
Space-clamped axon. Spikes start in the axon initial segment in real cells; here the spike and INaP share one compartment.
Generic kinetics. Gates use simple sigmoids and the A-type and Na⁺ activations are instantaneous. Spike shapes and rates are qualitative, not fitted to one cell.
Normalised drive. Currents are per unit area (µA/cm²), so “0.66” has no direct pA equivalent without assuming a membrane area.
No noise, no synapses. In vivo, background synaptic input and channel noise change how sharply the cell switches between patterns.

03 · WHY IT MATTERS

One synapse, two opposite effects
Hyperpolarising chloride: a 2 nS synapse arriving up to about 1 ms after the pulse onset vetoes the spike. Once the AIS has fired (from about 1.5 ms), the same synapse only delays the spike, by up to about 0.8 ms, and by 3 ms it has almost no effect. Chandelier control is a narrow timing window, not a constant brake.
Depolarising chloride: the synapse never blocks. Arriving before the pulse, it advances the spike (by up to about 2 ms at 20 nS). Arriving with or just after the pulse, its shunt slightly delays it. Whether chandelier cells are "excitatory" depends on the chloride gradient and on timing.
The debate is real. Cortical slice work reported excitatory axo-axonic effects (Szabadics et al. 2006), hippocampal measurements found hyperpolarising GABA along the whole axis including the AIS (Glickfeld et al. 2009), and in vivo hippocampal axo-axonic cells inhibit pyramidal cells during behaviour (Dudok et al. 2021).
Bridge to the fly: in the MANC connectome the AN08B098 (Axc) cells contacting the giant-fibre axon are predicted cholinergic, and activating them raised GF firing (Ceballos et al. 2026). Same anatomical motif, opposite sign: axo-axonic placement is a general way to gate spike output.
Next step for your axoaxonic-learning-model: this is that model's "deferred" item, a biological CA1 reconstruction, already running. Add the timing × conductance sweep with your EGABA values, or plasticity of AIS position (Pan-Vazquez et al. 2020).

04 · MODEL DETAILS

Under the hood
Under the hood cell, AIS, synapse, protocol
CELL

CA1 pyramidal mpg141209_A (Migliore et al. 2018 reconstruction, rat) with the Migliore et al. (2005) channel set (same as the active-dendrites page). The traced axon is replaced by a standard hillock (10 µm, 2 µm diameter), AIS (30 µm, 1.2 µm, Na⁺ 5× somatic) and axon (400 µm, 1 µm), so AIS geometry is controlled. Steady-state start at −65 mV.

SYNAPSE

One NEURON Exp2Syn at the AIS midpoint: \(g(t)=\bar g\,\frac{e^{-t/\tau_2}-e^{-t/\tau_1}}{\max}\), τ1 = 0.5 ms, τ2 = 8 ms, \(I = g(t)(V-E_{GABA})\). This lumps a chandelier cartridge (several boutons on one AIS) into a single conductance: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 14, 20 nS.

PROTOCOL

Rheobase for a 2 ms somatic pulse was found by bisection (0.7236 nA); the test pulse is 1.05× that. Δt = synapse onset − pulse onset: -10, -8, -6, -4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3 ms. Spike = somatic V crossing 0 mV; latency is measured from pulse onset. CVODE, 50 ms per trial, 260 trials.

LIMITS

A single cell and a lumped synapse. There is no Kv1 or Nav1.6/1.2 split at the AIS, and no realistic AIS chloride dynamics (EGABA is fixed per run). Spike threshold is measured at one stimulus strength. Use this to form hypotheses, then test them with AIS-specific channel models.

Method how Z(f), fR and Q are measured, and checks
PROTOCOL

Each model is first brought to its steady state at the holding current (analytic or numerical; the HH model is integrated for 8 s). For each frequency f a sinusoid A sin(2πft) is injected from that state (by default A is scaled so the largest predicted response is ≈ 0.25 mV, keeping every model in its linear range); the time step is adjusted to divide the period exactly; the first max(1 s, 3 cycles) are discarded as transient and the next max(4 cycles, 1 s), an integer number of cycles, are analysed. The voltage is fitted by least squares with a constant, a linear drift and sine and cosine terms at f and 2f: Z = (a + ib)/A, |Z| = amplitude/A, phase = atan2(b, a). Integration is fourth-order Runge–Kutta (Δt 0.05 ms; 0.025 ms for HH).

FR AND Q

fR is the frequency of the largest |Z|, refined by a parabola through the three highest points; if the largest |Z| is at the lowest frequency the model is non-resonant (fR = 0). Q = |Z(fR)| / |Z(fmin)|, the usual resonance strength with fmin the lowest frequency swept. A peak at the highest frequency is flagged: extend the range.

SUBTHRESHOLD CHECKS

Threshold and reset are disabled in the integrate-and-fire models. Each point reports the peak-to-peak response and the second-harmonic ratio; a point is flagged if a spike occurs (HH: V > −20 mV; AdEx: V > VT + 3 mV), if the response exceeds 5 mV peak-to-peak, or if the second harmonic exceeds 5 % of the fundamental and 0.01 mV (nonlinearity). A linear drift within the window (e.g. from seconds-long Iₕ) is fitted jointly so it does not bias the result. Lower the amplitude if flags appear.

IMPLEMENTATION CHECK

The line in Figure 2 is the model’s own linearisation: analytic admittances for the LIF, GLIF, NaP/Iₕ and AdEx models, and the exact Jacobian of all 11 variables for HH. Agreement within ~1 % at small amplitude confirms that the simulated equations, units and the measurement agree. The table reports the largest deviation.

Method spike detection, bursts, phase and statistics
TWO KINDS OF SPIKE

Action potentials (HH, Lowet minimal): the membrane equations generate the spike; it is detected when the somatic voltage crosses −20 mV upward and re-armed below −40 mV. Integrate-and-fire events (LIF, GLIF, NaP + Iₕ, AdEx): the model has no spike current; an event is recorded when V reaches threshold (Vth, Θ or Vpeak) and V is reset. Their timing is meaningful; their shape and width are not. Each table row states which kind it is.

BURSTS

Spikes closer than the threshold interval form one event; an event with ≥ 2 spikes is a burst. Ceballos et al. 2025 use 14 ms; Lowet et al. 2023 use 10 ms and report the same conclusions for 6–15 ms. A regular train faster than 1/threshold is counted entirely as bursts; this is flagged. Burst fraction = spikes in bursts / all spikes (the measure Lowet et al. report, 28 % in imaged CA1 cells).

PHASE LOCKING

For n events with phases φk, R = |Σ eiφk| / n (0 = no locking, 1 = perfect) and the mean phase is its argument. The Rayleigh test p-value uses Zar’s approximation p = exp(√(1 + 4n + 4(n² − (nR)²)) − (1 + 2n)). The γ band is 40 sinusoids at random frequencies in 30–90 Hz scaled to the RMS of a sinusoid of amplitude Aγ; its Hilbert transform is computed exactly from the same sum.

INTERVAL STATISTICS

CV = SD(ISI) / mean(ISI) (1 for a Poisson train, 0 for a clock). CV₂ = mean of 2|ISIk+1 − ISIk| / (ISIk+1 + ISIk) measures irregularity between neighbouring intervals and is insensitive to slow rate changes (Holt et al. 1996). Rheobase: the lowest current on the grid with a nonzero rate; gain: rate increase over the next 1 µA/cm².

BURST-MECHANISM CONTROL

With rhythmic input removed (only DC and noise) a model with an intrinsic burst mechanism still fires bursts; a model whose “bursts” are just high-rate moments at the θ peak does not. This separates the Lowet signature from simple rate modulation.

01 · REDUCE

From 11 variables to 2: derivative conductances

The lab’s reduction method (Pena, Ceballos, Lima & Roque 2018; Pena & Rotstein 2022). Hold the biophysical cell at a subthreshold steady state V*. Each gated current Ix = gxx(V − Ex) then splits into a chord conductance gxx* that acts instantly and a derivative conductance that acts through the gate’s time constant τx:

\[ G^{Der}_x = g_x\,(V^*-E_x)\,\frac{dx_\infty}{dV}\Big|_{V^*}, \qquad Z(\omega)=\Big[i\omega C + g_{L,\mathrm{eff}} + \sum_x \frac{G^{Der}_x}{1+i\omega\tau_x}\Big]^{-1} \]

A positive, slow GDer (IM, Iₕ) opposes voltage changes after a delay: a band-pass, resonant current. A negative one (INaP, KA inactivation) amplifies. Keeping only the dominant slow term gives the linear 2-D model C dv/dt = −gL,effv − g₁w + I, τ₁ dw/dt = v − w, which is exactly the subthreshold part of the 2-D AdEx (a = g₁, τw = τ₁).

01 · CHECK AGAINST THE PAPER

What reproduces, and what does not (yet)

Resonance sweeps of the biophysical model in the Python reproduction (hybrid reading, Iapp = 1, one 2 µA/cm² sinusoid into soma and dendrite, 4 s per frequency, 2–100 Hz). Each panel varies one conductance from the paper’s Fig 3 defaults (gNaP 0.93, gKdr 5.86, gₕ 8.46).

Figure 4. Resonant frequency of single spikes (fSS, blue) and bursts (fBS, purple) against gNaP, gKdr and gₕ. Bursts lock one per cycle in the 5–20 Hz band; single spikes win below ~5 Hz and in gamma.

PAPER FINDING	REPRODUCTION
Single spikes and bursts resonate at different, interleaved frequencies	Yes. Bursts: theta–beta (fBS 8–20 Hz); single spikes: gamma (fSS 25–45 Hz), plus a low-frequency single-spike band. Holds for the hybrid reading (gNaP 0.93) and for the lab-code reading at gNaP 0.3.
fSS above fBS for all gₕ	Yes. Both rise with gₕ (Δf 3 → 22 Hz from gₕ 0 to 16), because the slow Iₕ acts as a depolarising conductance.
Δf reverses sign with gNaP (SS above BS at low, below at high)	No. With θp = −35 mV, INaP is nearly closed between spikes, so gNaP barely moves either resonance. A sign that the authors’ exact θp or drive differs.
Δf reverses with gKdr (SS below BS at low gKdr)	No: fSS stays above fBS; at gKdr = 3 bursts disappear.
Burst peak rate always above single-spike peak (ΔA < 0)	No: ASS > ABS here, because bursts are capped at one per input cycle. The paper’s rate normalisation may differ.
Bursting appears near gNaP ≈ 0.35 under DC (Fig 1, one compartment)	Yes: single spikes up to 0.3, bursts from 0.35, CV > 2 at 0.5.
Bursts follow long silences; single spikes short ones (Figs 6–7)	Yes, qualitatively (Figure 5): γ alone gives only single spikes after < 50 ms silences; θ alone gives bursts only after ≥ 50–100 ms; θ + γ looks like θ alone. The absolute cut-off is lower than the paper’s 100 ms because a 10 Hz θ caps silences near 100 ms.

Figure 5. Probability that an event is a burst, against the silent interval before it (hybrid reading, Iapp 1, noise D = 0.2, 10 runs × 20 s, input to soma and dendrite). Bars of height ~0 mean events occurred but none were bursts; missing bars mean no events in that bin.

Which settings matter. Re-running Figure 4 under other readings: with input to the dendrite only, bursts nearly vanish; with the lab code’s Iₕ settings (gₕ 2, dendritic DC 0.9) the picture is unchanged. With the lab code’s θp = −47 mV and gNaP scaled to ~0.3 (the Fig 1–2 regime), gNaP now moves both resonances (fBS 20 → 30 Hz, fSS 40 → 70 Hz) and at low gKdr bursts outnumber single spikes (ΔA < 0), closer to the paper. So the gNaP and gKdr trends hinge on the θp and gNaP pair: the first thing to confirm.

Reading this honestly: the qualitative result is robust across readings, but the parameter dependences on gNaP and gKdr are not, which points at the open questions below (θp, input site and DC level). Those are the things to confirm with the authors before treating any one reading as the model.

02 · MEASURE

Two theta resonances: M near threshold, h near rest

Hu et al. (2002) found that CA1 pyramidal cells resonate at theta twice: an h-resonance at hyperpolarised potentials and an M-resonance at depolarised potentials, amplified by INaP. Here a small chirp current (0.5–20 Hz, 0.02 nA, 4 s) is injected at the soma at a chosen holding level and the impedance is measured for the full model, without Iₕ and without IM. Move the holding current to see which current carries the resonance.

What to expect. With the defaults, holding at −0.3 nA (≈ −73 mV) gives a resonance that disappears without Iₕ but not without IM; holding at +0.15 nA (≈ −61 mV) gives a much sharper resonance that collapses without IM. That is the voltage dependence Hu et al. (2002) reported. The peak frequencies here (15–20 Hz) are higher than the theta frequencies measured in slices, so the model captures which current resonates where, not the exact frequency.

CA1 circuit: theta, gamma and two output modes

Where CA1 pyramidal cells get theta and gamma from, which interneurons shape their timing, and a small network model that asks whether the single-cell result (bursts follow theta, single spikes follow gamma) survives inside a circuit.

Inputs
Interneurons
Theta and gamma

01 · INPUTS

Two excitatory pathways, two rhythms
PATHWAY	LANDS ON	RHYTHM IT CARRIES
CA3 → CA1 (Schaffer collaterals)	Radiatum and oriens dendrites	Slow gamma (~25–50 Hz) coupled to CA3 (Colgin et al. 2009)
Entorhinal cortex layer III → CA1 (temporoammonic)	Lacunosum-moleculare tuft	Fast gamma (~65–140 Hz) coupled to medial entorhinal cortex (Colgin et al. 2009); a major theta current generator (Buzsáki 2002)
Medial septum (cholinergic and GABAergic)	Interneurons and pyramidal cells	Paces theta, largely through interneurons (Buzsáki 2002)

02 · INTERNEURONS

Who inhibits which part of the cell, and when

Interneuron classes target different domains of the pyramidal cell and fire at characteristic phases of theta and gamma (Klausberger & Somogyi 2008). Quantitative cell counts and connection probabilities for CA1 are compiled in Bezaire & Soltesz (2013) and were used to build a full-scale CA1 network that generates theta from interneurons (Bezaire et al. 2016).

CLASS	TARGET ON THE PYRAMIDAL CELL	ROLE RELEVANT HERE
PV basket cells	Soma and proximal dendrites	Gamma rhythm generation; timing of single spikes
Axo-axonic (chandelier) cells	Axon initial segment	Control of spike initiation
Bistratified cells	Oriens and radiatum dendrites, alongside CA3 input	Gating of Schaffer input
OLM cells	Lacunosum-moleculare tuft, alongside EC input	Theta-rhythmic gating of entorhinal input; strong Iₕ
CCK basket cells	Soma	Behaviour-dependent, cannabinoid-sensitive inhibition

03 · THETA AND GAMMA

Rhythms and the two output modes

Theta (4–12 Hz) dominates the hippocampus during exploration (Buzsáki 2002); gamma is nested in it, with slow and fast gamma routing CA3 and entorhinal information at different theta phases (Colgin et al. 2009). Lowet et al. (2023) showed that in CA1 bursts phase-lock to theta and single spikes to gamma, and that 8 Hz versus 40 Hz optogenetic drive selectively increases bursts versus single spikes. The model work shows each mode has its own preferred frequency within one cell; the toy circuit below asks what happens when the rhythms come from inputs and interneurons instead of an injected sinusoid.

04 · TOY CIRCUIT

Pyramidal cells, PV and OLM interneurons, EC theta and CA3 gamma

The circuit runs live (default ¼× so you can follow the theta cycle); every slider acts immediately. Pyramidal cells are the AdEx fitted to the biophysical model (its slow variable is the linearised IM). EC input is theta-modulated; CA3 input is gamma-modulated with theta-nested amplitude and also drives PV cells; PV inhibits pyramidal somata, OLM cells give slow distal-like inhibition. This is a hypothesis-testing toy, not a calibrated CA1 model: rates correspond to in-field firing.

Locking is the vector strength (0 = none, 1 = perfect) of event times relative to the input cycle.

Bursts are theta-locked (vector strength 0.76 vs 0.42 for single spikes), as in Lowet et al. (2023). About a quarter of events are bursts, close to the ~28 % of spikes in bursts they report.
Single spikes are not the better gamma followers in the intact circuit. Bursts start at theta peaks, where theta-nested gamma is strongest, so they inherit gamma locking. With theta drive removed, single spikes lock to gamma (0.35) more than bursts (0.15). A testable prediction: the single-spike gamma preference should be clearest when theta input is weak.
The M current gives bursts their theta preference. Without it, rates triple and bursts lock to theta less than single spikes, consistent with IM as the slow variable that ends each burst (Golomb et al. 2006).
Removing PV inhibition raises the burst fraction (27 → 44 %); in AD mouse models PV interneurons are impaired (Verret et al. 2012), so this is one route by which the balance of output modes could shift.

03 · THE BIOLOGY

How CA1 place fields form, and why the output modes matter
Plateau potentials create fields in one trial. In head-fixed mice on a treadmill belt, a single dendritic plateau potential, spontaneous or evoked, produced a place field at that location on the next lap (Bittner et al. 2015, 2017).
BTSP works on a seconds-long window. Inputs active several seconds before or after the plateau are potentiated, more strongly before, so the new field’s ramp of depolarisation is asymmetric and starts before the plateau site (Bittner et al. 2017). The weight change is bidirectional and depends on the starting weight (Milstein et al. 2021).
Plateaus are dendritic Ca²⁺ events driving complex-spike bursts that need entorhinal input to the tuft (Takahashi & Magee 2009; Grienberger et al. 2014; Bittner et al. 2015).
Phase precession appears when a ramp of depolarisation combines with theta: the stronger the drive, the earlier in the cycle threshold is reached (Harvey et al. 2009; O’Keefe & Recce 1993).
Bursts carry more spatial information than single spikes and precess more strongly (Lowet et al. 2023), consistent with bursts following theta-paced input in the field and single spikes following gamma.
In Alzheimer’s models CA1 place fields are less stable and spatial coding degrades (e.g. Cacucci et al. 2008); how much of this is a change in BTSP or in the balance of bursts and single spikes is an open question that this kind of model can frame.

03 · THE MODEL

What is simulated, and what is simplified
\[\dot v=0.04v^2+5v+140-u+I_{syn}+I_{bias},\quad \dot u=a(bv-u),\quad v\ge 30\ \text{mV}\Rightarrow v\leftarrow c,\ u\leftarrow u+d\]\[I_{syn}=\sum_{exc}w\,e^{-(t-t_k-\delta)/3\,\mathrm{ms}}-\sum_{inh}w\,e^{-(t-t_k-\delta)/7\,\mathrm{ms}},\qquad \delta=0.8\ \mathrm{ms}+\frac{\text{distance}}{v_{axon}}\]
Neurons: 299 Izhikevich point neurons (regular-spiking pyramidal and granule cells, bursting CA3 cells, fast-spiking interneurons, slower O-LM cells) plus 60 entorhinal Poisson inputs.
Delays: each connection’s delay is the distance on the slice map (1 unit ≈ 4 µm) divided by an axonal speed of 0.3–0.4 mm/ms, plus 0.8 ms synaptic delay.
Where inhibition lands: point neurons have no dendrites, so location is approximated: axo-axonic inhibition is the strongest (it acts at the spike initiation site), and O-LM inhibition divides the entorhinal input to CA1 rather than subtracting, mimicking shunting in the distal tuft.
Scaled down: rat CA1 alone has about 311,500 pyramidal cells in the Bezaire model; here there are 80. Convergences are scaled down from the data below while keeping their proportions roughly; DG and CA3 parameters are illustrative.
For real multiscale work: the full-scale CA1 network (Bezaire et al., 2016, ModelDB 187604) and detailed cells from the atlas can be run in NEURON; NetPyNE and the Blue Brain hippocampus models build networks from reconstructed morphologies.

06 · DO IT IN PYTHON

The same idea in NumPy: a feedforward chain with delays
Python 3 · numpy, matplotlib
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
dt, T = 0.1, 120.0                                  # ms
pops = {"EC": 30, "DG": 120, "CA3": 60, "CA1": 80}
names = list(pops); start = np.cumsum([0] + list(pops.values()))
N = start[-1]
a = np.full(N, 0.02); b = np.full(N, 0.2); c = np.full(N, -65.0); d = np.full(N, 8.0)
v = np.full(N, -65.0); u = b * v
# feedforward connections: (pre, post, in-degree, weight, delay ms)
conns = [("EC", "DG", 10, 5.2, 6.0), ("DG", "CA3", 4, 16.0, 4.0), ("CA3", "CA3", 6, 2.2, 1.5), ("CA3", "CA1", 12, 2.6, 4.0), ("EC", "CA1", 8, 2.0, 6.0)]
D = 120; buf = np.zeros((D, N)); edges = []
for pre, post, K, w, dly in conns:
    for j in range(start[names.index(post)], start[names.index(post) + 1]):
        for i in rng.integers(start[names.index(pre)], start[names.index(pre) + 1], K):
            edges.append((i, j, w, int(round(dly / dt))))
out = [[] for _ in range(N)]
for i, j, w, k in edges: out[i].append((j, w, k))
e = np.zeros(N); spikes = []
for step in range(int(T / dt)):
    t = step * dt
    e += buf[step % D]; buf[step % D] = 0
    I = e.copy()
    ec = slice(0, pops["EC"])
    fired_ec = (rng.random(pops["EC"]) < (0.04 if 20 <= t < 24 else 0.0001))   # entorhinal burst at 20 ms
    v += dt * (0.04 * v**2 + 5 * v + 140 - u + I); u += dt * a * (b * v - u)
    fired = v >= 30; fired[ec] = fired_ec
    for i in np.flatnonzero(fired):
        spikes.append((t, i)); v[i] = c[i]; u[i] += d[i]
        for j, w, k in out[i]: buf[(step + k) % D, j] += w
    e -= dt * e / 3.0

t, i = np.array(spikes).T
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3)); plt.scatter(t, i, s=2, c="k")
for k, n in enumerate(names): plt.axhline(start[k], lw=0.5, c="grey"); plt.text(1, start[k] + 3, n)
plt.xlabel("time (ms)"); plt.ylabel("neuron"); plt.title("A burst travels EC → DG → CA3 → CA1")
for n in names:
    s = t[(i >= start[names.index(n)]) & (i < start[names.index(n) + 1]) & (t > 20)]
    print(f"{n}: first spike at {s.min() - 20:.1f} ms after the burst" if s.size else f"{n}: silent")

WHAT’S HAPPENING NOW

Schaffer collaterals. The spike travels 1.29 mm along the drawn axon (≈ 3.7 ms). 60 synapses land on CA1 trunk, obliques and basal dendrites, on average 152 µm from the soma, so each adds only ≈ 0.19 mV at the soma. Together they reach -54.0 mV, below the −52 mV threshold. Increase the number of CA3 cells firing together or turn off feedforward inhibition.

Feedforward inhibition. The basket cell fires at 7.9 ms and inhibits the CA1 soma ≈ 1 ms later. Excitation that has not summed to threshold by then is cut short: a narrow window for coincidence detection.

Under the hood every synapse, its NEURON kernel, and the parameters used

02 · THE CALCULATION

How each step is computed
\[V_{soma}(t)=V_{rest}+\sum_i \frac{I_i}{50\,\mathrm{pA}}\,K_{s(i)}\,\alpha(t-t_i)-\mathrm{IPSP}(t),\qquad \alpha(u)=\frac{u}{\tau_{s(i)}}e^{1-u/\tau_{s(i)}}\]

Ks and τs: somatic EPSP peak (per 50 pA) and time-to-peak for a synapse on section s, from NEURON.

Spike in the presynaptic cell. It travels along the drawn axon at 0.35 mm/ms (unmyelinated hippocampal axons conduct at roughly 0.2–0.5 mm/ms) and reaches each synapse after a 0.8 ms synaptic delay. Spikes from the group of presynaptic cells are jittered by ±0.5 ms.
Synapses are placed on real dendritic segments in the layer each pathway targets: Schaffer collaterals on CA1 trunk and obliques in radiatum, mossy fibres on proximal CA3 apical dendrite (stratum lucidum), entorhinal input on the CA1 tuft.
Passive spread to the soma. For each synapse the somatic EPSP amplitude and time-to-peak are taken from a passive NEURON model of the reconstruction (precomputed for every dendritic section). The pink wave you see uses the simpler e−d/λ picture for display.
Summation and threshold. Rest −65 mV, threshold −52 mV. Each synapse’s somatic EPSP comes from a NEURON simulation of that exact reconstruction (see Under the hood): synaptic currents of 15 pA (Schaffer, entorhinal) give somatic EPSPs of roughly 0.1–0.3 mV; mossy-fibre terminals (400 pA) give several mV.
Feedforward inhibition. The basket cell gets the same Schaffer input but fires earlier in its integration (fast, low threshold), then inhibits the CA1 soma about 1 ms later. It narrows the window in which inputs can sum (Pouille & Scanziani, 2001).

This is a teaching calculation, not a compartmental simulation: no active dendritic channels, dendritic spikes or plateau potentials (which can make distal input much more effective; Takahashi & Magee, 2009). To run the real thing, load these reconstructions into NEURON with the ModelDB models linked in the atlas.

03 · NUMBERS TO CHECK AGAINST

How many inputs does it take?
CA3 → CA1: single Schaffer synapses give somatic EPSPs of a fraction of a millivolt, so dozens of CA3 cells must fire together. In the full-scale CA1 model each pyramidal cell receives about 5,985 CA3 connections (Bezaire et al., 2016).
DG → CA3: each CA3 cell receives only a few dozen mossy-fibre inputs, but each is strong and facilitating, so a handful of granule cells firing in a burst can make a CA3 cell fire.
EC → CA1: tuft synapses are far from the soma. On their own they barely move it in a passive cell; real tufts use dendritic spikes, and timing with Schaffer input matters.

03 · HOW IT WAS CHECKED

Under the hood
Under the hood coordinates, region tests and what was excluded
COORDINATES

The meshes are Allen CCFv3 (2017) structure meshes (structure IDs: root 997, HPF 1089, CA1 382, CA2 423, CA3 463, DG 726, SUB 502, ENTl 918, ENTm 926, MS 564, TH 549, Isocortex 315, CB 512, STR 477, OLF 507), re-decimated by vertex clustering to 80–300 µm. The neurons are the MouseLight Source-Version SWC files from NeuroMorpho.Org, in CCF µm. Their axes (ML, DV, AP) were reordered to the mesh axes (AP, DV, ML). The CNG versions on NeuroMorpho are re-oriented, so they cannot be placed in the atlas.

REGION TEST

Point-in-mesh uses the generalised winding number: \(w(p)=\frac{1}{4\pi}\sum_{t}\Omega_t(p)\), where \(\Omega_t\) is the solid angle of triangle \(t\) seen from \(p\). A point is inside when \(|w|>0.5\). This is robust to the small holes that decimation leaves.

EXCLUDED: SEU–ALLEN CELLS

Four SEU–Allen full-morphology cells (Peng et al. 2021) are in the neuron atlas, but not here. When their source coordinates were read as 25 µm CCF voxels, the CA1 and CA3 somata landed in isocortex (ventral posteromedial nucleus: TH; CA1: Isocortex; CA1: CA3; CA3: Isocortex). Their frame needs a transform I could not verify, so they are not drawn rather than drawn in the wrong place. Their total lengths do match NeuroMorpho (103 and 130 mm).

Each of the two giant fibers (DNp01) has dendrites in the brain, where visual looming and other inputs arrive. Its very large axon descends through the neck (cervical connective) into the ventral nerve cord (VNC).

In the second thoracic neuromere each GF drives two outputs:

TTMn (tergotrochanteral motor neuron) → TTM jump muscle. This is a mixed synapse: ShakB gap junctions plus a cholinergic chemical component.
PSI (peripherally synapsing interneuron) through gap junctions. PSI then excites the DLM flight-muscle motor neurons with a cholinergic synapse.

The GF is a descending neuron. In the VNC its axon also receives input onto the axon itself (axo-axonic synapses), mostly from ascending neurons (AN) and local interneurons (IN). That is what the Peña lab analysis maps.

Measured latencies (stimulate GF, record muscle; Allen & Murphey 2007): TTM 0.85 ± 0.03 ms, DLM 1.43 ± 0.07 ms. Without gap junctions (shakB²), TTM is 1.62 ± 0.17 ms, follows only 17.5% of pulses at 100 Hz and 10.5% at 250 Hz, and DLM does not respond.

06 · DEVELOPMENT & GENETICS

How the giant synapse is built
shaking-B encodes an innexin gap-junction protein. shakB² mutants lack functional GF–TTMn and GF–PSI gap junctions (Phelan et al. 1996; Thomas & Wyman 1984). This leaves the slow, labile chemical TTM response and no DLM response.
The chemical component is cholinergic: cha-GAL80 removes GF labelling; chaᵗˢ² and tetanus toxin abolish the residual TTM response (Allen & Murphey 2007).
GF morphology and synapse development are described across pupal stages by Allen, Drummond & Moffat (1998).
Neuroglian (L1-CAM homologue) is needed for GF–TTMn synapse formation, and human L1-CAM can substitute (Godenschwege et al. 2006). Neuroglian interacts genetically with Semaphorin-1a during guidance and synapse formation (Godenschwege & Murphey 2009).
Pathways around the GF

Descending neurons (≈1,300 DNs in MANC) carry brain commands to the VNC; the GF is one of them. Ascending neurons report leg and body state back to the brain, and many of them also contact DN axons in the VNC. In your export, ANs supply 357 of 800 axonal synapses (45%). Ceballos et al. found axo-axonic DN connections in about 1 % of possible pairs, organised as a decentralised “broker” network.

How to read the figure. Left: the lumbar spinal cord in cross-section (dorsal = back at the top). 04 · FOR TEACHERS

Learning goals and discussion questions
Trace the pathway: receptor → afferent → synapse → motor neuron → efferent → NMJ → muscle → movement, and estimate each delay.
Explain why myelinated axons conduct faster (saltatory conduction) and predict the effect of demyelination on reflex timing.
Describe synaptic transmission at the NMJ: Ca²⁺-dependent, quantal ACh release (release ∝ [Ca²⁺]⁴), nicotinic receptors, AChE, and a large safety factor.
Link the muscle action potential to Ca²⁺ release (DHPR–RyR), troponin/tropomyosin, cross-bridge cycling and relaxation by SERCA; explain summation and tetanus.
Explain reciprocal inhibition: why the hamstrings relax while the quadriceps contract.
Compare a monosynaptic reflex (knee-jerk) with a polysynaptic one (withdrawal from a pin), including crossed extension in the other leg.
Download student worksheet + answer key

The worksheet is a printable HTML file. Its answer key is filled in with numbers from this model, run at the default settings.

Discussion: Why does a reflex not need the brain? Why can lowering external Ca²⁺ weaken the kick even though the nerve still fires? Why is the NMJ “fail-safe” in a healthy person but not in myasthenia gravis? What happens to force if Ca²⁺ were not pumped back?
